questions.question:
Parts of the given sentence have been given as options. One of them contains a grammatical error. Select the option that has the error.

As long as there was corruption in India, there can be no progress.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is** "there was corruption"** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** We will here see the grammatical error with the help of the whole sentence:

__
 
• As long as*** there was corruption ***in India, there can be no progress.​
 
• "is" should be used in place of "was"

**Correct sentence**: As long as there **is **corruption in India, there can be no progress.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**Now let's understand the correct sentence formation:

 
• It should be **there is corruption** instead of **there was corruption.**
 
• We use **"is" **in the present tense whereas we use** "was" **in the past tense.
 
• More specifically, we use** "is"** in present continuous tense
 
 
• Eg. He *is* eating food.
 
 
 
• On the other hand, the verb** "was"** is used in past continuous tense
 
 
• Eg. The bird *was *flying to its nest.

questions.question:
Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence.

I don’t get on with the new boss, so I __have asked to transferring__ to another branch of the company.

options.text: will have ask to be transfer
have been ask to be transferring

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **"have asked to be transferred"** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 Let's see the correct sentence formation:

__
 
• I don’t get on with the new boss, so I*** have asked to be transferred ***to another branch of the company.​

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**Let's how the correct sentence formation happens:

 
• It should be** ****have asked to be transferred** instead of **have asked to transferring**
 
• Grammatically speaking,** "be"** is an auxiliary verb, and** "to be" **is its infinitive format.
 
• Regarding the meaning, both kind of mean the same.
 
• They can both convey the existence or occurrence of something, possessing a quality, or just simply show a particular tense without having an independent meaning.
 
• Talking about** "ed"** and **"ing" **in the words **"transferred"** and **transferring"**
 
• Adjectives ending in **-ed** show what has happened to a person or thing.
 
• Adjectives ending in **-ing** show the effect which something has on a person or thing.

questions.question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

Usnis has not used the computer for weeks.

options.text: The computer did not used by Usnis for weeks.
The computer has not been used by Usnis for weeks.
The computer was not been used by Usnis for weeks.
The computer has not being used by Usnis for weeks.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **"The computer has not been used by Usnis for weeks"**** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__**​Let's see the passive formation:

__
 
• **Usnis has not used the computer for weeks* (passive voice)*** 

 
 
• The computer has not been used by Usnis for weeks ​
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**Let's learn about passive voice:

 
• **Passive voice -** The passive voice, the subject is acted upon by some other performer of the verb
 
• 
 
In a **passive voice construction**, the grammatical subject of the clause receives the action of the verb.

 
 
• 
 
***The formula:***

 
 
• 
 
**[subject]+[some form of the verb to be]+[past participle of a transitive verb]+[optional prepositional phrase]**

 
 
• 
 
***Eg***. The ball was kicked by Chester.

 
 
 
 
• That last little bit—“by Chester”—is a prepositional phrase that tells you who the performer of the action is. But even though Chester is the one doing the kicking, he’s no longer the grammatical subject. A passive voice construction can even drop him from the sentence entirely
 
 
• ***Eg.*** The ball was kicked.
